Current Visual Question Answering (VQA) models excel in answering questions on images, but their limited reasoning capabilities prevent them from being applied to real-world problems where multiple visual entities are involved. To overcome this challenge, we introduce a novel approach that enables VQA models to reason multi-entity interactions more effectively. Our approach is based on the concept of "entity interactions" that are defined by the relationships between visual entities, and it uses a simple yet efficient method to reason their interactions in answering visual question. To demonstrate the efficacy of our approach, we conduct comprehensive experiments on the HICO-Dataset, a benchmark for Heterogeneous Object-Centric Settings, and our results show that it significantly outperforms existing methods by achieving a higher score of 38.9% with a noticeable improvement in reasoning multi-entity interactions. The associated code and pre-trained models are available for download on https://github.com/chenruofan/hico_with_interactions.

This research presents an innovative approach to recognizing emotion in speech, 
utilizing acoustic features translated into images, subsequently fed into a 
deep learning model for classification. A convolutional neural network (CNN) 
was employed for image classification, demonstrating an impressive 89% accuracy 
on the original dataset prior to further refinement and expansion of its 
acoustic and visual content. Following this, an ensemble model consisting of 
LSTM networks was trained on the expanded dataset, yielding a 93% accuracy rate 
without overfitting. To further enhance performance, data augmentation was 
implemented, resulting in a non-significant enhancement to the accuracy rate. 
When evaluated on the original dataset, recognition rates of 87.8%, 91.7%, 
and 96.4% accuracy rates for boredom, disgust, and happiness respectively, were 
achieved. Notably, this methodology outperformed existing state-of-the-art models 
utilizing similar datasets, indicating its superior effectiveness. Additional 
analysis revealed that removing specific features, such as energy and spectral 
roll-off, did not compromise the model's accuracy rate, suggesting that these 
features may not be crucial for successful emotion recognition. Ablation study 
findings suggest that features like formant ratio and spectral roll-off are more 
significant for accurate emotion classification. This methodology's superior 
accuracy rates, along with its interpretability, highlight its potential as a 
superior emotion recognition approach. An accompanying video demonstrating this 
methodology's results can be accessed at https://youtu.be/6L8L8L8L8L8. A 
companion repository containing the code for this research is available at 
https://github.com/avastcloud/emotion-speech. This research's findings were 
presented in the 2021 ICASSP conference, held in Melbourne, Australia.

the title "Emotional speech recognition using acoustic features and CNN" which can be 
found at https://arxiv.org/abs/2101.04629. A separate paper detailing the model's 
enlargement and performance enhancement is available at 
https://arxiv.org/abs/2110.04251. A third paper presenting the ablation study is

This research focuses on a scenario where multiple agents in a dynamic network compete for limited resources. Each agent has a specific objective and can make decisions based on current conditions and predictions about future outcomes from a given set of options. The collective value that the agents would achieve if they collectively made an optimal choice is defined as a competitive equilibrium social welfare. Additionally, this study examines the competitive equilibrium social welfare in a competitive scenario where agents act selfishly, revealing that it is the maximum welfare that can be achieved under a collective optimal approach. Based on this insight, the concept of competitive equilibrium learning is introduced to enable agents to learn and adapt to their environment by making decisions that maximize their individual welfare. The learning approach is further refined to account for uncertainty and noise in the environment, resulting in a robust learning algorithm that can converge to the optimal welfare even in the presence of noise. The effectiveness of this learning algorithm is demonstrated through experiments on a synthetic problem, where it is shown to outperform other popular reinforcement learning methods. Moreover, this learning algorithm is shown to achieve faster convergence than other methods when faced with changing environmental conditions. The competitive equilibrium learning framework is also applied to a multi-agent scenario where agents learn to navigate a dynamic environment, demonstrating the effectiveness of this approach in achieving optimal welfare under changing conditions. The initial state of the proton in the proton-proton collision is altered by the presence of a photon, which then affects the distribution of partons and the resulting jet production. This distortion leads to modifications in jet characteristics, specifically $p_T$ spectra and $R$ distributions. To investigate these effects, we employed a Monte Carlo simulation that incorporates a photon-induced distortion of the initial proton state, using a parton shower program and PYTHIA8 as our tool for analysis. Our results indicate that the influence of the photon on jet production is minimal, yet it does have a noticeable impact on certain jet characteristics, particularly when considering the effects of initial-state radiation. This effect can be further enhanced by increasing the photon's energy and jet radius. Additionally, we observed that the photon's influence on jet production is more pronounced in proton-photon collisions compared to proton-proton collisions. Our findings suggest that the modification of jet characteristics by the presence of a photon can provide valuable insights into the initial state of the proton. This, in turn, can be leveraged to improve our understanding of proton structure by analyzing jet production at particle colliders. Finally, we propose that the study of proton-proton collisions with and without a photon could offer a means of distinguishing between different models of proton structure. This distinction would be particularly relevant in cases where the proton's partonic structure varies across different energy scales. This research delves into the effects of strain on the charge density waves in transition metal dichalcogenides. We apply a unique transformation technique to the electronic structure of these materials and reveal new insights into the relationships between strain, charge density waves, and the electron-phonon interaction. As a result, we identify a previously unknown phase transition in 1T-WSe2, where the charge density wave transitions from a n(n+1)/2 to a n+1 phase under tensile strain. Moreover, we discover that the onset of this transition occurs at a strain threshold of approximately 1.5%, marking a significant milestone in the control of charge density waves using strain manipulation. Our findings also shed light on the potential of strain tuning in modifying charge density waves and other correlated systems. Additionally, we demonstrate the possibility of using strain to induce superconductivity in 1T-WSe2, where the material exhibits a 2D Dirac dispersion, by introducing a phonon-mediated attraction between electrons. Our research provides a comprehensive framework for the design of strain-assisted devices that exhibit tunable charge density waves and superconductivity. Finally, we discuss the implications of our findings for the experimental detection of these phenomena in transition metal dichalcogenides. This paper presents a rigorous analysis of the Momentum method and Adam optimization technique, treating them as stochastic differential equations. By deriving their learning rules from this analysis and comparing them to their original formulas, we investigate their performance under various conditions. Specifically, we investigate the impact of different learning rates and batch sizes on these algorithms, finding that they match their original descriptions when using a novel variance estimator. Furthermore, we find that the Momentum method outperforms Adam when the learning rate is high and the batch size is small, but Adam performs better with a balanced learning rate and batch size. Overall, our results validate the original descriptions of these algorithms, but also highlight the limitations of these formulations, particularly in scenarios with varying learning rates. Consequently, we propose an alternative stochastic differential equation that describes Adam's dynamics, leading to a simplified expression for the learning rate. When compared to existing formulations, our result is more general and applicable to a wider range of scenarios. These findings are supported by experiments conducted on various datasets, including MNIST, CIFAR-10, and NLP tasks such as GLUE and SuperGLUE benchmarks. The advancement of conversational AI has led to the development of sophisticated utterance classification models, capable of identifying specific intentions behind user input. Although deep learning models excel in this domain, they often struggle to apply learned knowledge to novel, unseen situations. This discrepancy highlights a significant challenge in the field of conversational AI research. This study investigates the effectiveness of various training methods in enhancing deep learning models' adaptability to unfamiliar domains. Four training approaches are examined: human observer feedback, where a model is trained using labeled data and corrective feedback; crowdsourced examples; crowdsourced examples combined with human observer feedback; and crowdsourced examples with human observer feedback and additional artificial data generated through GANs. The results demonstrate that models benefit significantly from human observer feedback and crowdsourced examples, but indicate that additional artificial data does not significantly improve performance. This research contributes a comprehensive evaluation of multiple training methods for utterance classification models, highlighting key findings and potential avenues for future research. We introduce an innovative, automated process to generate parameter-dependent reduced-order models (ROMs) that utilize deep neural networks (DNNs). This process, which is grounded in the ROM construction method known as POD/DMD, involves the following key components: initially, we perform model reduction on a given model to obtain a low-dimensional representation of its parameter space. Subsequently, we use DNNs to create non-parametric ROMs that effectively capture the relationships between the ROM and the original model. This process is demonstrated using various examples from different application areas, where we compare the performance of our new method to traditional ROM construction methods. Notably, our results show that the DNN-based ROMs we generate achieve comparable accuracy to these traditional ROMs while requiring significantly less computational resources. Moreover, our new method offers a unique advantage by allowing for the generation of accurate ROMs that can be trained using limited data, thereby overcoming the need for extensive, expensive simulations. As such, this approach has the potential to be widely applied across a variety of fields including physics, engineering, and economics. This shift has resulted in the separation of web applications into multiple client and server components, which has significantly impacted web development and maintenance. However, the use of client or server-side applications has increased the complexity of web systems and raised concerns about their scalability and cost. This research aims to investigate the impact of cross-context communication on web applications, specifically how different communication methods can affect their performance and maintainability. A comparative analysis was conducted of two popular communication methods, REST and WebSocket, which were applied in different contexts to evaluate their impact on web development. The results showed that cross-context communication using WebSocket led to improved performance and faster response times, while the choice of communication method influenced the structure and placement of web services, impacting both the design and maintenance of web applications. This research contributes to our understanding of web development by exploring the implications of cross-context communication for web systems. The findings can inform the development of web applications that are faster, more cost-effective, and easier to maintain, while also providing guidelines for web developers to make informed decisions about communication methods and system design. A recent pandemic has led to a dramatic shift in global priorities, with a consequent impact on scientific funding. To gauge the effects on this funding, we analyzed a substantial dataset from over 11,000 research grants totaling around 6 billion dollars awarded in the US, UK, and UK, and discovered a significant surge in support for COVID-19 related research, with a concomitant decline in funding for other areas such as climate change. Our findings show that while basic biomedical research has been somewhat protected, emergency response initiatives and vaccine development have become priorities. Additionally, we found a correlation between COVID-19 and climate change, with research in these two areas now increasingly intertwined. Our study highlights the need for strategic funding of scientific research during emergencies, with a focus on accelerating the research process without compromising on research quality. However, we also recommend that funders prioritize long-term research initiatives, especially in areas like climate change, to ensure a more sustainable funding balance in the future. Ultimately, we propose that the COVID-19 pandemic has created an opportunity for a more holistic approach to scientific research, one that protects vulnerable communities and environments while also advancing human capabilities. We believe that by working together, we can seize this opportunity to drive positive change in the world. A legal expert system is proposed that autonomously identifies the relevant legal basis using a comprehensive database of German law. The system achieves this by simulating a question-and-answer interview, where the user's input is analyzed through a natural language processing algorithm to create a case tree. This tree is then systematically matched with relevant legal sections, which are subsequently ranked based on how well they fit. Ultimately, the system identifies the most suitable legal basis by eliminating any inconsistencies and resolving any ambiguities. In a real-world scenario, the system can serve as an effective tool for corporate legal departments or legal aid hotlines. Furthermore, it has the potential to simplify the legal process by narrowing down relevant information and allowing users to submit applications online. Evaluations conducted using a dataset of 300 cases revealed that the system achieved an accuracy rate of 80% in identifying relevant legal sections. The results demonstrate the feasibility of fully automating the application process, while also highlighting areas for further research. The legal basis identification system is now available to the public and can be easily integrated into other applications. In this study, we identify a fundamental pattern in the radical series of Bol algebras and leverage this pattern to establish a connection between Bol algebras and Malcev algebras. Utilizing this connection, we demonstrate that a finite-dimensional Bol algebra has a finite-dimensional center and that the center's dimension does not exceed the dimension of the algebra. Furthermore, we derive a classification of Bol algebras that are self-representations of Bol algebras over division rings. The proposed approach was also found to enhance security and stability in the power system operation. Furthermore, it was observed that using real-time forecasts instead of historical data resulted in a 5% decrease in the operating cost of the power system. The proposed approach was also found to be computationally efficient, with a solution time of 0.1 seconds on a personal computer. We introduce a named-entity recognition (NER) task tailored to the specific needs of mathematics, which focuses on identifying the key components of theorem and corollary statements while also capturing their provenance information. Our approach utilizes an extended version of the CONLL-UPOS tagging scheme and builds upon it by incorporating additional tags to distinguish between theorems, corollaries, and their respective numbers. The E-MATH-Net corpus, a large dataset of mathematical papers sourced from MathSciNet, serves as the foundation for our experiments. Our results demonstrate the efficacy of a transformer-based NER model in analyzing this dataset, achieving a high F1 score of 99.2%. Furthermore, we demonstrate the ability to apply our model to an automatically generated dataset, one that is created by extracting and annotating theorem and corollary content from Wikipedia articles. Our approach yields a satisfactory F1 score of 98.4% on this generated dataset. Our goal is to establish a foundation for advanced mathematical text analysis techniques, including theorem categorization, which we aim to leverage in the development of advanced search engines and information retrieval systems for the mathematical community. Our approach also offers the potential to facilitate theorem reconciliation, enabling the correction of known results and the discovery of novel ones. The theorem recognition models we have developed are publicly available for use and extension at https://github.com/gsaghatanabbi/thm-ner. The associated code is also compatible with the Transformers library, enabling the integration of our models into a range of deep learning frameworks. We address the challenge of recovering 3D geometry from a single 2D portrait image. Our approach builds upon the concept of Neural Radiance Fields, which have recently shown great potential in reconstructing detailed geometry from multiple images. However, these methods typically require a large number of images, making them unsuitable for practical applications. Our key contribution is a meta-learning framework that leverages transfer learning to adapt the Neural Radiance Fields model for a specific portrait image based on a large database of corresponding 3D geometry representations. This allows us to effectively utilize the knowledge gained from the database to fit the model efficiently for a single image, achieving high-quality geometry estimates in the process. Our results demonstrate significant improvements over baseline methods, especially when working with limited image data. Moreover, our approach can be easily extended to generate realistic 3D geometry from a single image, enabling the creation of animated 2D silhouettes. Specifically, we show that for any function defined within this expanded logical framework, if it is continuous, a specific sequence of rational numbers converging to the function's limit can be systematically constructed. Conversely, we demonstrate that for any sequence of rational numbers converging to a limit, a symbolic function f can be systematically defined such that it equals this limit, along with a symbolic proof of this equivalence. Furthermore, we establish a method to calculate the limit of a function f based on its total variation, provided f is expressible within this expanded logical framework. Ultimately, we apply our findings to symbolic logic with additional elements for handling ordinal and cardinal numbers, in addition to the ability to express limited quantifications. This enables us to calculate the limit of a function f mapping natural numbers to natural numbers, provided f is expressible within this expanded logical framework, along with a symbolic proof of this equivalence. A visual recording of sunspot data has been a long-standing practice in astronomy, yet it lacks the precision of some of the more advanced methods employed today. Researchers have delved into the historical sunspot records, discovering that the data contains a wealth of information, including not only the observations themselves, but also the individual observers and their cultural backgrounds. This paper examines the evolution of sunspot data across multiple cultures, highlighting the potential for biases and inaccuracies, such as different recording systems and techniques. It also investigates the role of personal background characteristics on the accuracy of the data. Utilizing a database of 18th and 19th century sunspot records from a diverse range of cultures, the study reveals that the data contains a range of systematic errors, including undercounting sunspots and a tendency for observers to record larger spots. The results of this research have significant implications for our understanding of the Sun during the Maunder Minimum, during a period of significantly reduced solar activity. It is hoped that this study will contribute to a more accurate understanding of the Sun's past behavior and serve as a valuable resource for future researchers. Finally, the paper includes a detailed analysis of the life and contributions of James Watson, a Scottish astronomer who made significant sunspot observations and was a key figure in Scottish astronomy during the 18th century. Watson's observations were particularly notable during the Maunder Minimum period, during which he recorded the longest unbroken series of sunspot data. Although Watson's life remains largely unexplored, the study reveals that his data has been consistently reliable and accurate, making him an important figure in the field of astronomy. This research paper is part of a broader initiative to create a comprehensive historical database of sunspot data, which will be used to reconstruct the Sun's past behavior over the past 400 years. A related database initiative is also underway to create a comprehensive historical atlas of the Sun, featuring a series of hand-drawn illustrations of the Sun's appearance during different periods. This atlas is expected to be completed in 2023. Both databases are expected to be publicly accessible online. CDE is formulated as a center-aware depth prediction problem, where the task involves predicting depth around the image center and surrounding edges. A dual-branch network architecture is designed to tackle these two aspects, with a center-aware depth prediction branch predicting depth around the image center and an edge-aware depth prediction branch predicting depth around the edges. A new center-aware depth loss function is also proposed to enhance the accuracy of the center-aware depth prediction branch. Experimental results on multiple depth estimation benchmarks demonstrate the effectiveness of the CDE method in achieving state-of-the-art performance. This research focuses on constructing and analyzing the Chern forms of higher rank coherent analytic sheaves over complex algebraic varieties. Specifically, we demonstrate that smooth Chern forms can be combined to create a Chern current for such sheaves. We examine the dynamic characteristics of a quantum heat engine operating under time-varying conditions, focusing on scenarios in which the energy source undergoes periodic fluctuations. This engine can be represented using a non-equilibrium steady state description, which enables us to derive a general expression for its work output. By considering different energy input types, we establish a trade-off between efficiency and power output, and also investigate the thermodynamic implications of working in or beyond stationary states. Furthermore, we introduce a comprehensive quantum thermodynamic efficiency metric and measure it for various types of quantum heat engines, revealing a connection between high efficiency and high coherence in certain cases. The impact of system coherence on its thermal and energy characteristics is also explored. Using a two-level system as an energy source, we demonstrate how coherence can be leveraged to create an engine with a specific power-speed trade-off, and also present a detailed analysis of a quantum heat engine's performance close to third-law efficiency limits. Finally, we investigate the performance of a quantum heat engine operating between two non-equilibrium states. By employing a quantum harmonic oscillator as a model system, we show that this engine can be made more efficient by increasing the energy disparity between the two states, and that its performance is influenced by the coherence of the system's quantum state. These results have the potential to inform the development of advanced heat engines. Recent breakthroughs in self-supervised learning have led to the development of highly effective methods for pre-training CNNs, resulting in impressive performance across a range of downstream tasks. Despite this progress, the underlying principles of self-supervised learning remain poorly understood. This study proposes the frequent data bias hypothesis, suggesting that self-supervised learning primarily learns to identify common features associated with frequently occurring data points. This idea is substantiated by a thorough analysis of the Imagenet dataset, which reveals a substantial correlation between data frequency and the features learned by self-supervised models, particularly those incorporating frequent data augmentation patterns. Furthermore, the research demonstrates that self-supervised models trained on Imagenet subsets exhibit enhanced generalizability on tasks characterized by significant class imbalance, a phenomenon that is explicitly validated through targeted experiments. These findings offer a new perspective on the existing understanding of self-supervised learning and provide valuable insights for the ongoing pursuit of more effective self-supervised learning approaches. This research introduces a cutting-edge neural network-based approach to enhance speaker localization accuracy in complex environments. The method relies on an external microphone to generate a binary filter, and integrates this into an existing multi-microphone setup. This allows an initial neural network to pinpoint the direction of the external microphone, and subsequently apply the resulting binary filter to fine-tune the primary network's performance. The technique was thoroughly tested on diverse datasets featuring a range of speaking directions, resulting in substantial improvements in localization precision, notably up to 28%. Moreover, the proposed method demonstrates adaptability to various performance standards, offering notable enhancements even in less chaotic environments. The code supporting this research is made available for review and further development.

The spread of divisive ideologies within a social network has become a pressing concern. To address this issue, we have developed a comprehensive framework for assessing the level of polarization in a social group. Our framework is based on two key concepts: the diversity of opinions (DO) and the density of active connections (DOr), which are calculated from the network structure and the beliefs of its members. DO measures the extent of diverse opinions within the network, while DOr quantifies the density of connections between individuals with opposing views and reveals the presence of polarizing influences. Human motion tracking in virtual reality and free-viewpoint capture relies on accurate 3D human pose estimation. Conventional approaches utilizing RGB images and LiDAR data are limited to short periods, typically less than a minute, due to challenges in calibrating and registering LiDAR data. Alternatively, Inertial Measurement Unit (IMU)-based methods can provide precise 3D poses locally, but are less accurate over extended periods. We propose a novel framework that integrates RGB images, LiDAR data, and IMU data to estimate human pose both locally and globally. Our approach involves a two-stage process, first fusing IMU and LiDAR data to generate 3D poses and then combining the LiDAR data with the predicted poses to obtain human joint locations. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our method in tracking human pose over extended periods, as shown in our experiments using data from the Human3.6M dataset and real-world recordings. The code and accompanying data are available on GitHub. The 3D human pose estimation results show that our method outperforms existing methods in tracking human pose over extended periods, with a median error of 0.56Meas and 0.81Meas in real-world and simulated datasets respectively. Furthermore, our method can be used to track human pose in a more realistic setting by combining the estimated 3D poses with the depth map, with a median error of 0.51Meas in the simulated dataset. This research investigates the use of vision transformers (ViTs) for generating bird's eye view (BEV) maps, which is a novel application of ViTs. Based on these findings, we introduced a hybrid model that combines the strengths of ViTs and Convolutional Neural Networks. Our experimental results show that this model can generate highly detailed BEV maps, which can be used to improve object detection and other tasks. This study introduces a groundbreaking approach to anomaly detection, capable of identifying novel class instances even when none from the labeled class have been seen before. By contrast, existing methods typically rely on labeled data from known classes to generate artificial samples for detection. Our proposed Out-Of-Sighted Learning approach generates these artificial samples by distorting the input signal in a way that preserves the spatial distribution of the original signal, effectively creating an adversarial example for the target class. This innovation enables the detection of unknown class instances without access to known class data, as demonstrated through experiments on multiple datasets, including CVUSA, MVT, and AFAD, which show our method outperforms existing solutions. Furthermore, comprehensive ablation studies and a series of baseline experiments have been conducted to validate the effectiveness of our approach. Our findings indicate that the proposed Out-Of-Sighted Learning method surpasses existing alternatives in unknown class detection tasks. Evaluating the correlation structure of stationary time series is crucial, 
especially in scenarios with varying stationarity, where models like piecewise 
stationary time series are more suitable as they account for both correlations 
and structural changes. However, traditional inference methods may not be reliable 
under high noise conditions. In this study, a semiparametric approach is 
proposed to infer piecewise stationary time series with multiple segments. 
By utilizing the Hilbert-Schmidt independence criterion, the proposed method 
estimates the time-varying correlation function and achieves accurate and 
efficient results under high noise conditions. The proposed method also exhibits 
excellent performance in comparison to other popular methods. Additionally, the 
method's potential is illustrated through an analysis of a high-dimensional time 
series dataset. The proposed method's implementation is provided in the R package 
psTS. This package can be accessed at the repository at https://github.com/ps-ts/psTS.

This paper reports on our system's submission to the 2020 ASVINS challenge, which involves generating authentic responses to social engineering prompts. Our primary objective was to enhance the efficiency of our data-driven approach by refining question and framing identification, thereby improving the quality of our responses. By integrating a classification module that distinguishes between questions and framing, we were able to generate more convincing responses. Furthermore, we developed a method to predict and reconfigure the order of responses to make them more coherent and natural. Our results demonstrate that manually reordering our data in specific ways enables our system to produce more effective and engaging social engineering content, leading to a notable system win with the highest established score of 46.4. Our system's performance was evaluated using a large set of professionally crafted social engineering scenarios and prompts. Our findings also highlight the significance of improving ask and framing detection in data-driven approaches to generate more authentic responses. In addition, we provide insights into the system's architecture and its ability to produce high-quality content at high speeds, with a processing rate of 1000 queries per second. Our code is now publicly available for further research and development on the GitHub platform. Ultimately, we believe that our work showcases the potential of combining rule-based and data-driven methods to generate more effective social engineering content. This research presents a novel cost constructor that can handle occlusions by creating a refined cost map from a set of depth estimates, thereby improving depth estimation accuracy. The constructor is trained in an unsupervised manner using a weakly supervised approach, where a deep network is learned to remove noise from a cost map generated by another network, based on binary labels provided. The training process involves two-step refinement: first, the network is trained to remove noise from a cost map generated by a pre-existing cost constructor, thereby refining the cost map and improving depth estimation, then the noise removal process is repeated to further refine the cost map, leading to even better depth estimates. Experiments demonstrate that the proposed approach outperforms existing methods in depth estimation. The research also explores the benefits of using this approach for complex scenes with extensive occlusions, where state-of-the-art cost constructors fall short.
